title: Designing a thread-safe class: immutable, confinement, delegation, locking strategies
shortTitle: How do you design a thread-safe class?
keyPoints: Immutability is the best strategy: if nothing changes, nothing can be corrupted. Records and final fields are inherently thread-safe.
Thread confinement means state is never shared: stack-local variables and ThreadLocal give each thread its own copy.
Delegation means using existing thread-safe classes (ConcurrentHashMap, AtomicInteger) instead of writing your own synchronization.
Locking with synchronized or Lock is the last resort: guard all shared mutable state with a consistent lock.
Anti-patterns include synchronized(this) (exposes lock), synchronized(new Object()) (creates a new lock each time), and leaking mutable internal state.
Always prefer the simplest strategy that works: immutability before confinement before delegation before locking.

s1_definition.oneliner: Design thread-safe classes using four strategies in order of preference: immutability, confinement, delegation to thread-safe classes, and locking as a last resort.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Immutability** – no mutable state at all. If nothing changes, nothing can be corrupted. Strings, records with immutable fields, and `BigDecimal` are examples. Zero synchronization needed.
- **Confinement** – mutable state is never shared between threads. Each thread has its own copy via stack-local variables or `ThreadLocal`. No sharing means no race condition.
- **Delegation** – delegate to existing thread-safe classes like `ConcurrentHashMap`, `AtomicInteger`, `LongAdder`, and `BlockingQueue`. Let well-tested library code handle synchronization.
- **Locking** – guard all shared mutable state with a consistent lock: `synchronized(privateFinalLock)`. This is the most error-prone strategy and should be used only when the others do not fit.
s1_definition.analogy: Immutability is like a printed bank statement: nobody can change it, so you can hand it to 100 people with zero risk. Confinement is like each teller having their own calculator: nobody shares, so nobody fights over it. Delegation is like buying a professional vault (ConcurrentHashMap) built by experts with built-in security: do not build your own vault. Locking is like building a custom safe with your own padlock: it works, but you might forget to lock it or hold the key too long.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Thread-Safety Strategy Preference Order:

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  1. IMMUTABILITY                         │  Best: zero synchronization
  │     final fields, records, String        │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  2. CONFINEMENT                          │  Good: no sharing
  │     stack locals, ThreadLocal            │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  3. DELEGATION                           │  Good: expert-built safety
  │     ConcurrentHashMap, AtomicInteger     │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  4. LOCKING                              │  Last resort: error-prone
  │     synchronized(privateFinalLock)       │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Thread-safe class design follows four strategies in preference order. Immutability is the best: if nothing changes, nothing can corrupt. Records with immutable fields are freely shareable across threads with zero synchronization. Confinement is next: stack-local variables and `ThreadLocal` give each thread its own copy, eliminating sharing entirely. Delegation comes third: use `ConcurrentHashMap`, `AtomicInteger`, and `BlockingQueue` instead of writing your own synchronization. Locking is the last resort: `synchronized(privateFinalLock)` guards shared mutable state, but is the most error-prone approach.

The anti-patterns are equally important: `synchronized(this)` exposes the lock to external code. `synchronized(new Object())` creates a new lock every time, providing no synchronization at all. Returning mutable internal state from a getter lets external code corrupt your data.

Remember one sentence: prefer immutability over confinement over delegation over locking, and always use a private final lock object when locking is necessary.
